rabindranath-tagore: Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May 1861 in the Jorasanko mansion in Calcutta, the youngest of 13 surviving children of Debendranath Tagore and Sarada Devi. His mother died in his early childhood, and he was raised mostly by servants. The family was at the forefront of the Bengal Renaissance, hosting literary magazines, theatre and recitals of Bengali and Western classical music. Tagore wrote poetry at eight, and at sixteen published poems under the pseudonym Bhanusimha that literary authorities took for long-lost classics.

Tagore wrote novels, essays, short stories, travelogues, dramas and thousands of songs. He is credited with originating the Bengali short story. Gitanjali, Gora and Ghare-Baire are his best-known works, and his compositions became the national anthems of India and Bangladesh. In 1912 he took translations of his works to England, where William Butler Yeats, who wrote the preface to the English Gitanjali, and others noticed them.

He opposed imperialism and supported Indian nationalists, yet he rebuked strongly nationalist forms of the independence movement. In 1925 he attacked the Swadeshi movement in an essay, The Cult of the Charkha. He urged the masses to seek self-help and education rather than blind revolution, and his religious and philosophical ideas appear in the 1922 lectures Creative Unity and the 1931 Hibbert Lectures at Oxford, published as The Religion of Man.

Tagore conceived a new kind of university to make Santiniketan a connecting thread between India and the world. He named it Visva-Bharati; its foundation stone was laid on 24 December 1918, and teaching was often done under trees. He died on 7 August 1941 at Jorasanko Thakur Bari, the house in which he was born.
ranoji-scindia: Ranoji Scindia, also known as Ranoji Sendrak, was born about 1700 into a Maratha family. His father, Jankoji Rao I, was hereditary patil, or village head, of Kanherkhed, a village in the present Satara district of Maharashtra. In earlier centuries his forefathers had served as shiledars, cavalrymen, under the Bahmani Sultanate, and had held jagirs. As a young man he entered the service of Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath. Ramchandrababa Sukhtankar, one of the Peshwa's diplomats, recognised his talents and had him made personal bodyguard to the Peshwa's son, Baji Rao I.

When Baji Rao was appointed Peshwa at the age of twenty by Chhatrapati Shahu, the appointment aroused the jealousy of senior officials at the Maratha court. He therefore promoted talented young men, barely out of their teens, to command his troops, among them Ranoji Scindia, Malhar Rao Holkar, the Pawar brothers, Pilaji Jadhav and Fateh Singh Bhosle. None of them came from families that had held hereditary deshmukhi rights under earlier rulers such as the Deccan Sultanates.

Ranoji was in charge of the Maratha campaign that Baji Rao began in Malwa in 1726, and after it he established his capital at Ujjain in 1731. He appointed Ramchandrababa Sukhtankar as his dewan, or administrator, and Yashaji Rambhaji as commander of his army, and himself spent most of his life on campaign. Some historians credit him with bringing the Kumbh Mela to Ujjain in 1732.

Ranoji died on 3 July 1745. He had five sons: Jayappa Rao, Jyotiba Rao, Dattaji Rao, Tukoji Rao and Mahadji. The four eldest died in battles in northern India between 1750 and 1761. The dynasty went on to dominate central and northern India in the later 18th century through its presence at Delhi, its collection of chauth from neighbouring rulers and a modernised army, and his descendants ruled the princely state of Gwalior under the British.
rashid-ali-al-gaylani: Rashid Ali was the son of Sayyid Abd al-Wahhab al-Gailani and belonged to a prominent Baghdad family whose name points to an origin in Gilan in Iran and which traces its ancestry to the Prophet Muhammad; he also descended from Circassian governors of the Ottoman period. He studied at the law school in Baghdad and practised as a lawyer before entering politics.

In 1924 Yasin al-Hashimi made him minister of justice in his first government, and he was elected president of the Chamber of Deputies in 1925 and 1926. Both men were nationalists opposed to any British part in Iraq's internal politics. They rejected the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty signed by the government of Nuri as-Said in 1930 and formed the Party of National Brotherhood. Gaylani was prime minister for the first time from March to November 1933.

He returned to the premiership on 31 March 1940, after the early death of King Ghazi, when Emir Abdul-Illah was regent for the four-year-old Faisal II. Gaylani refused Allied troops passage through Iraq, rejected calls to break with Fascist Italy and sent his justice minister, Naji Shawkat, to Ankara, where on 5 July 1940 he met the German ambassador, Franz von Papen. Britain imposed economic sanctions, and under pressure from the regent he resigned on 31 January 1941.

With the Golden Square he then planned to assassinate the regent, who discovered the plot on 31 March and fled. The coup followed on 1 April, and on 3 April a National Defence Government took office under Gaylani. He sent artillery against the RAF base at Habbaniya. On 2 May the base's commander struck first at the Iraqi positions; within a week the Iraqis left the escarpment, and British forces advanced through Fallujah on Baghdad. Gaylani fled to Iran on 30 May. An armistice was signed the next day, and the regent returned on 1 June. Immediately afterwards the Farhud, a violent pogrom against Jews, took place in Baghdad.

After British and Soviet forces invaded Iran on 25 August 1941 he went on to Italy and then Berlin, where Adolf Hitler received him and he was recognised as leader of an Iraqi government in exile. On Germany's defeat he found refuge in Saudi Arabia. He returned to Iraq only after the revolution of 1958 that overthrew the monarchy, plotted a revolt against the government of Abdul Karim Kassem and was sentenced to death. Pardoned in July 1961, he lived in Lebanon, where he died on 28 August 1965 at the age of 72.
rene-descartes: René Descartes was born in La Haye en Touraine, in the Province of Touraine, on 31 March 1596. His mother, Jeanne Brochard, died in May 1597, a few days after giving birth to a stillborn child, and he lived with his grandmother and great-uncle. His father, Joachim, was a member of the Parlement of Rennes. In 1607, late because of his fragile health, he entered the Jesuit College of La Flèche, where he was introduced to mathematics and physics. He then studied at the University of Poitiers and took a degree in canon and civil law in 1616, as his father wished.

His Discourse on the Method of 1637 introduced essays on optics, meteorology and geometry. The Meditations on First Philosophy followed in 1641, and the Principles of Philosophy, a Latin textbook meant to replace the Aristotelian ones used in universities, in 1644. The Discourse appeared in a single edition of 500 copies, and the French edition of the Meditations had not sold out by his death, but a Latin edition of the Meditations was a commercial success. He died on 11 February 1650.

Descartes used hyperbolic doubt: he rejected any idea that could be doubted, then tried to rebuild knowledge on a firm foundation. The first principle he reached was that he thinks, expressed as cogito, ergo sum, or I think, therefore I am. Since doubting needs a doubter, the fact of doubt proved his existence. He concluded that perceiving his body through the senses was unreliable evidence, and that the only indubitable knowledge was that he is a thinking thing.

In mathematics he and Pierre de Fermat developed analytic geometry, which uses algebra to describe geometry; the Cartesian coordinate system is named after him. He is credited with representing unknowns by x, y and z and with using superscripts for powers. In his Principles he stated three laws of motion and claimed that the total quantity of motion in the universe is conserved, and Isaac Newton's laws were later modelled on his exposition. By shifting the question from what is true to what he could be certain of, he is often called the father of modern Western philosophy.
republic-of-serbian-krajina: The name Krajina, meaning frontier, came from the Military Frontier that the Habsburg monarchy carved out of Croatia and Slavonia between 1553 and 1578 against the Ottoman Empire. In the 1991 census Serbs made up about 12.2 per cent of the population of Croatia. After Franjo Tuđman was elected president of Croatia in April 1990, the Serb Democratic Party of Jovan Rašković broke with the Croatian parliament. In August 1990 Serbs blocked roads with logs in what became known as the Log Revolution, cutting Dalmatia off from the rest of the country, and a referendum confined to Serbs backed Serb sovereignty and autonomy by 99.7 per cent.

The Croatian constitution of December 1990 reduced the Serbs from a constituent people to a national minority. On 21 December 1990 the administration of Milan Babić announced a Serbian Autonomous Oblast of Krajina, which on 1 April 1991 declared that it would secede from Croatia.

Wider war began in August 1991. Between August and December approximately 80,000 Croats were expelled and some were killed; estimates of all exiled Croats and other non-Serbs range from 170,000, the figure of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, to a quarter of a million, that of Human Rights Watch. On 19 December 1991 the autonomous oblasts of Krajina and Western Slavonia proclaimed the republic, and that of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia was added on 26 February 1992.

The Vance plan and the Sarajevo Agreement of January 1992 established four United Nations Protected Areas and froze the front lines for three years. Refugees were not allowed to return. Babić, who opposed the plan, was replaced as president on 26 February 1992 by Goran Hadžić; Milan Martić won the presidency in January 1994. The economy depended wholly on the rump Yugoslavia: by 1994 only 36,000 of 430,000 citizens were employed. Croatian forces took Western Slavonia in Operation Flash in May 1995.

In Operation Storm between 150,000 and 200,000 Serbs fled, and only 5,000 to 6,000, mostly elderly, remained; some who refused to leave were murdered, tortured or expelled by the Croatian army and police. The remaining territory in eastern Slavonia was placed under a United Nations transitional authority by the Erdut Agreement and returned to Croatia in 1998.

The tribunal sentenced Babić, who pleaded guilty, to 13 years in 2004 and Milan Martić to 35 years in 2007. The Croatian generals Ante Gotovina and Mladen Markač were convicted in April 2011 of crimes during Operation Storm and acquitted on appeal in November 2012.
republic-of-the-congo: The Republic of the Congo lies on the western coast of Central Africa, west of the Congo River, along the Equator. It is bounded by Gabon, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Angolan exclave of Cabinda, and has 170 kilometres of beaches on the Atlantic. The southwest is a coastal plain drained by the Kouilou-Niari River, and the interior is a central plateau between two basins. The climate is consistent year-round, with a dry season from June to August.

The country is named after the Congo River, whose name derives from Kongo, a Bantu kingdom at its mouth around the time the Portuguese first arrived in 1483 or 1484. It is a distinct country from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its capital, Brazzaville, is named for the colony's founder, Pierre Savorgnan de Brazzà. Under France it was known as the French Congo or Middle Congo.

Bantu-speaking peoples mostly displaced and absorbed the earlier inhabitants, the Pygmy peoples, about 1500 BCE. By the 13th century there were three main federations of states in the western Congo Basin: the Seven Kingdoms of Kongo dia Nlaza in the east, Mpemba to its south, and a confederation of Vungu, Kakongo and Ngoyo to the west across the Congo River. The Tio Kingdom formed in the 14th century. The association of kingship with smithing is believed to have originated among the Tio before spreading to Loango and Kongo.

The Portuguese explorer Diogo Cão reached the mouth of the Congo in 1484, and trade grew between the inland kingdoms and European merchants, who dealt in commodities, manufactured goods and enslaved people. The area north of the river came under French sovereignty in 1880 through Pierre de Brazza's treaty with the Tio king Iloo I, and Iloo's widow, Queen Ngalifourou, upheld its terms. In 1908 France organised French Equatorial Africa, with Brazzaville as federal capital. The Congo–Ocean Railway, built after the First World War, has been estimated to have cost at least 14,000 lives.

The Republic of the Congo became independent from France in 1960 and was a Marxist–Leninist state under the name People's Republic of the Congo from 1969 to 1992. Its capital is Brazzaville. French is the official language, with Kituba and Lingala as national languages, and the Kongo are the largest ethnic group, roughly half of the population. Most of the population lives in the southwest, in Brazzaville, Pointe-Noire and the towns along the railway that joins them.
rio-de-janeiro: Rio de Janeiro lies near the west end of a strip of Brazil's Atlantic coast, close to the Tropic of Capricorn, where the shoreline runs east and west, so the city faces largely south. It was founded at the entrance to an inlet, Guanabara Bay, which is marked by a point of land called Sugar Loaf. The city occupies 1,182.3 square kilometres, and its residents are known as cariocas. Its parks include the Tijuca National Park, a national park since 1961, and the Passeio Público, described as the first public park in the Americas.

The region was inhabited by the Tupi, Puri, Botocudo and Maxakalí peoples. Europeans first encountered Guanabara Bay on 1 January 1502 during a Portuguese expedition, which gave the bay and then the city its name, meaning January River. In 1555 some 500 French colonists under Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon occupied an island in the bay and built Fort Coligny, attempting to found the colony of France Antarctique. The Portuguese saw it as a threat, and from 1560 a long military campaign led by Governor General Mem de Sá and later his nephew Estácio de Sá ended on 20 January 1567 in the defeat and expulsion of the French.

Estácio de Sá founded the city proper on 1 March 1565 and named it São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro, after the patron saint of the Portuguese king Sebastião. Until early in the 18th century it was threatened or invaded by pirates and buccaneers, mostly French. In 1763 it became the capital of the State of Brazil, and in 1808 the Portuguese royal court moved there. Rio remained the capital of the Portuguese monarchy until 1822, the only instance in modern history in which the capital of a colonising country officially shifted to one of its colonies. It then served as capital of the Empire of Brazil until 1889, and of republican Brazil until 1960, when the capital moved to Brasília.

Rio de Janeiro is the capital of the state of Rio de Janeiro, with about 6 million people in the city proper. It is known for its carnival, samba and bossa nova, and for beaches such as Copacabana and Ipanema. Landmarks include the statue of Christ the Redeemer on Corcovado, Sugarloaf Mountain and the Maracanã Stadium.
romania: Romania lies on the lower course of the Danube and on the northwestern shore of the Black Sea. It covers 238,397 square kilometres, and its terrain is distributed roughly equally between mountains, hills and plains. The Carpathian Mountains dominate the centre, with 14 ranges reaching above 2,000 metres; the highest is Moldoveanu Peak at 2,544 metres. They are surrounded by the Moldavian and Transylvanian plateaus, the Pannonian Plain and the Wallachian plains.

The Danube flows into the Black Sea and forms the Danube Delta, the second-largest and best-preserved delta in Europe. At 5,800 square kilometres it is the largest continuous marshland in Europe. Romania has one of the largest areas of undisturbed forest in Europe, covering almost 27% of its territory, and about 50% of Europe's brown bears outside Russia.

Human remains from Peștera cu Oase, about 40,000 years old, are the oldest known Homo sapiens in Europe. Salt production at the Poiana Slatinei site began between the 5th and 4th millennium BCE, the earliest evidence for salt exploitation in Europe, and the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture flourished in the 3rd millennium BCE. Greek colonies were established on the Black Sea coast in the 7th century BCE. Burebista, the first Dacian ruler to unite the local tribes, conquered the Greek colonies in Dobruja between around 55 and 44 BCE, and his kingdom collapsed after he was murdered in 44 BCE.

Part of the territory became the Roman province of Dacia after Trajan's Dacian Wars. The modern state was formed in 1859 through the union of Moldavia and Wallachia under Alexandru Ioan Cuza and took the name Romania in 1866. The Great Union of 1918 and the treaties that followed created Greater Romania, which reached its largest territorial extent. King Michael I was forced to abdicate in December 1947, and the communist Romanian People's Republic followed. The revolution of 1989 ended communism.

Romania is a semi-presidential republic with a bicameral Parliament of a Senate and a Chamber of Deputies. It joined the European Union in 2007 and is a member of NATO. The 2021 census counted 19,053,815 people, of whom 89.33% were Romanians, 6.05% Hungarians and 3.44% Roma; the Council of Europe puts the Roma figure higher, at 8.32%.

The name derives from the endonym român, from Latin romanus. The oldest surviving document in Romanian is Neacșu's letter of 1521, which mentions Țeara Rumânească, the Romanian Land, meaning Wallachia. About 12 million Romanians and people with Romanian-born ancestors live abroad.
rome: Rome lies in the Lazio region of central Italy on the Tiber. The original settlement developed on hills facing a ford beside the Tiber Island, the only natural ford of the river in this area. The Rome of the Kings was built on seven hills: the Aventine, Caelian, Capitoline, Esquiline, Palatine, Quirinal and Viminal. The city centre is about 24 kilometres inland from the Tyrrhenian Sea, though the city territory extends to the shore at Ostia.

The Aniene, which flows into the Tiber north of the historic centre, also crosses modern Rome. Vatican City, the smallest country in the world, is an independent country within Rome's municipal boundaries, the only existing example of a country within a city.

Evidence of human occupation of the Rome area goes back approximately 14,000 years. The view that Rome grew from pastoral settlements on the Palatine Hill, above the future Roman Forum, is supported by several excavations. Today there is wide consensus that the city developed gradually through the aggregation of several villages around the largest, on the Palatine, and archaeological evidence places this in the mid-eighth century BCE. The view that Rome was founded deliberately then, as the legend of Romulus suggests, remains a fringe hypothesis.

By 550 BCE Rome was the second largest city in Italy after Taras, with an estimated population of 35,000, though other sources suggest nearly 100,000. When the Republic was founded in 509 BCE the census recorded 130,000, and the city surpassed 300,000 by 150 BCE. After the fall of the Western Empire the city slowly fell under the political control of the Papacy, and in the 8th century it became capital of the Papal States, which lasted until 1870. Rome became the capital of the Kingdom of Italy in 1871.

Rome is the capital of Italy and a special municipality named Roma Capitale, with a population of 2.7 million. It hosts the country's principal political institutions and several United Nations agencies, including the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme. Its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Beginning with Nicholas V (1447 to 1455), almost all popes pursued an architectural and urban programme over four hundred years, and Rome became a major centre of the Renaissance and the birthplace of the Baroque and Neoclassicism. Its first university, La Sapienza, was founded in 1303. In 98 CE, according to Sextus Julius Frontinus, Rome had nine aqueducts feeding 39 monumental fountains and 591 public basins.
ronald-reagan: Ronald Wilson Reagan was born on 6 February 1911 in an apartment in Tampico, Illinois, the younger son of Nelle Clyde Wilson and Jack Reagan. His mother was committed to the Disciples of Christ and led prayer meetings; Reagan credited her spiritual influence. His father focused on making money for the family, a task complicated by his alcoholism. The family lived in several Illinois towns before settling in 1920 in Dixon, where Reagan attended Dixon High School and developed interests in drama and football. He graduated from Eureka College in 1932 with a degree in economics and sociology.

Reagan began as a sports broadcaster in Iowa, and a screen test in 1936 led to a seven-year contract with Warner Bros. Pictures. He arrived in Hollywood in 1937 and made thirty films, mostly B films, before beginning military service in April 1942. His part as George Gipp in Knute Rockne, All American (1940) later led reporters to call him the Gipper while he campaigned for president. He served as an officer in the Army Air Forces, producing over 400 training films, and was discharged on 9 December 1945 as a captain. He began his political life as a Democrat, admiring Franklin D. Roosevelt, and registered as a Republican in 1962 after General Electric dropped him as a speaker.

He was elected governor of California in 1966 and served from 1967 to 1975. He accepted tax increases to balance the budget, and by 1973 the state had a surplus. In 1967 he signed the Mulford Act, which prohibited the public carrying of firearms. After losing the 1976 Republican primaries to President Gerald Ford, he won the nomination in 1980 and defeated President Jimmy Carter. He was inaugurated as the 40th president on 20 January 1981. His economic policy, called Reaganomics, combined deregulation with tax cuts, including the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981, and he lifted federal oil and gasoline price controls on 28 January 1981.

Reagan left the presidency on 20 January 1989, at the age of 77, and the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library opened in 1991. He was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 1994, and his capacities gradually deteriorated. He died of pneumonia, complicated by Alzheimer's, at his home in Los Angeles on 5 June 2004. A public funeral was held in the Washington National Cathedral, where Margaret Thatcher, Brian Mulroney, George H. W. Bush and George W. Bush gave eulogies, and he was interred at his presidential library. His tenure is regarded as a realignment toward conservative policies in the United States.
ronnie-brunswijk: Ronnie Brunswijk was born on 7 March 1961; his birth village was Moiwana. He joined the Suriname National Army at the age of 18, was considered a good soldier and was sent to Cuba for commando training, after which he was appointed a personal bodyguard of Desi Bouterse. In 1984 he asked for a raise; instead he was discharged on 16 April and refused his back pay. He then sought recognition and rights for the Maroons of the interior, descendants of Africans who had escaped slavery and founded independent communities in the 17th and 18th centuries.

The Surinamese Interior War began at Stolkertsijver on 22 July 1986, when the Jungle Commando captured twelve soldiers guarding a checkpoint. During the war the group received arms and funding from the Netherlands. On 29 November 1986 the Surinamese army attacked Moiwana, murdered at least 39 villagers, mostly women and children, and burned Brunswijk's house; the Inter-American Court of Human Rights later ordered the government to compensate the survivors. The war caused hundreds of deaths and drove more than 10,000 refugees into French Guiana. A ceasefire was negotiated at Kourou on 21 July 1989, and a final peace treaty was signed on 8 August 1992.

A Dutch court in Haarlem convicted Brunswijk in absentia of cocaine smuggling and sentenced him to eight years' imprisonment, reduced to six years on appeal in 2000; he contested the evidence. He chairs the General Liberation and Development Party and has sat in the National Assembly. He owned a gold-mining company, Robruns NV, whose concessions he transferred to a foundation in July 2020 in order to qualify for the vice-presidency.

In the 2020 elections Brunswijk was elected to the National Assembly, and on 29 June 2020 he became its chairman. On 13 July he was elected vice-president by acclamation, with Chan Santokhi as president, and was inaugurated on 16 July. He also owns the football club Inter Moengotapoe and in 2002 built a stadium in Moengo. On 21 September 2021 he played 54 minutes for the club in the CONCACAF League against C.D. Olimpia of Honduras, aged 60 years and 198 days. After a video showed him paying Olimpia players, CONCACAF disqualified both clubs and banned him from its competitions for three years.
rurik-dynasty: Modern scholars consider Rurik a legendary and perhaps entirely fictional figure. The Primary Chronicle, of the early twelfth century, tells of the Calling of the Varangians: tribes at war with one another invited three brothers from overseas to rule them, of whom Rurik settled in Novgorod, Sineus at Beloozero and Truvor in Izborsk. No earlier Kievan source knew of Rurik, and genealogies of the princes usually stopped with Igor of Kiev. Even if Rurik existed, scholars have long doubted or rejected that he was Igor's father.

Before the mid-15th century no source claims that Rurik founded a dynasty. The tradition was set out by churchmen in the 16th century, in the Book of Royal Degrees of 1560 by Macarius, Metropolitan of Moscow, which traced the ruling house of Moscow to Rurik and to a supposed kinsman of Augustus Caesar named Prus. For this reason some scholars prefer the name Volodimerovichi, descendants of Volodimer I of Kiev.

The house underwent a major schism after the death of Yaroslav the Wise in 1054, dividing into branches descended from his sons Iziaslav, Sviatoslav and Vsevolod. By the middle of the twelfth century Kievan Rus' had dissolved into independent principalities, each under a different branch. Vsevolod's line, the Monomakhovichi, named after Vladimir II Monomakh, became predominant. The Olgovichi, descended from Sviatoslav, ruled in Chernigov until the early 14th century. The Romanovichi, the line of Roman the Great, were crowned kings of Galicia and Volhynia and ruled until 1323.

In the north-east the Yurievichi descended from Yuri Dolgorukiy, the founder of Moscow. His great-grandson was Alexander Nevsky, whose son Daniel of Moscow founded the ruling house of Moscow, the Daniilovichi. In all, the house ruled for 21 generations in the male line, a period of more than 700 years. It was briefly revived in Vasili IV of Russia, of the Shuyskiy line, who died without issue. The Time of Troubles lasted until 1613, when Mikhail I founded the Romanov dynasty; his father was descended from the Rurikids through the female line.

Russian and Ukrainian historians have long debated the inheritance of Kievan Rus'. The Russian view treats the Principality of Moscow as its sole heir, resting largely on religious and historical claims. The Ukrainian view of succession, summarised most clearly by Mykhailo Hrushevsky in his History of Ukraine-Rus', is based on continuity through the Kingdom of Ruthenia, Lithuania-Ruthenia and the Cossack Hetmanate. Several branches of the family survive, among them the houses of Shakhovskoy, Gagarin and Lobanov-Rostovsky.
russia: Russia is the largest country in the world, spanning eleven time zones and sharing land borders with fourteen countries. It stretches over the easternmost part of Europe and the northernmost part of Asia, some 9,000 kilometres from east to west, and is one of only three countries bordering three oceans. The Ural Mountains, running north to south through the west, form the traditional boundary between Europe and Asia. Mount Elbrus in the Caucasus, at 5,642 metres, is the highest peak in Russia and Europe, and Klyuchevskaya Sopka on the Kamchatka Peninsula is the highest active volcano in Eurasia.

Human settlement on Russian territory dates back to the Lower Paleolithic. The East Slavs became prominent in Europe between the 3rd and 8th centuries, and Kievan Rus' was established in the 9th century, adopting Orthodox Christianity from the Byzantine Empire in 988. After it disintegrated in the 12th century the Grand Principality of Moscow became the dominant Russian principality and led the unification of Russian lands, culminating in the Tsardom of Russia in 1547. Peter the Great proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721, which became the third-largest empire in history.

The Russian Revolution of 1917 abolished the monarchy and created the Russian SFSR, the first socialist state. After the Russian Civil War it became the principal constituent of the Soviet Union, established in 1922. Amid rapid industrialisation in the 1930s, millions died under Joseph Stalin. The Soviet Union played a decisive role for the Allies on the Eastern Front in World War II, then competed with the United States as a superpower during the Cold War. In 1991 the Russian SFSR emerged from the dissolution of the Soviet Union as the Russian Federation.

Russia had an estimated population of 146 million in 2025, and three-fourths of its people live in urban areas. Moscow is the capital and Saint Petersburg the second-largest city. A constitution adopted after a constitutional crisis in 1993 established a semi-presidential republic. Russian is the official language, and about 81% of the population were ethnic Russians in the 2010 census.
